source.title: Quadratic models for understanding catapult dynamics of neural networks
source.authors: Libin Zhu; Chaoyue Liu; Adityanarayanan Radhakrishnan; Mikhail Belkin

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices. The title metadata says 2022, but the text identifies it as published at ICLR 2024.
record.tranche_reason: Tests catapult dynamics using neural quadratic models and wide neural networks, with a different model formulation from the original learning-rate studies.
record.gate_note: The paper studies squared-loss optimization and catapult dynamics, not classification error. CIFAR-2 means a two-class subset of CIFAR-10. Values in the cited dynamics plots are figure-only; cited findings from prior work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study tests V5 through proofs for neural quadratic approximations and its own squared-loss gradient-descent experiments on wide ReLU networks. It establishes or reports catapult convergence and decreasing tangent-kernel eigenvalues; it is not an original source of V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors prove catapult dynamics for specified neural quadratic models and empirically show parallels with finite-width neural networks in optimization and generalization, arguing that quadratic approximations capture behavior missed by linear approximations.
record.recipe_differences: Uses squared-loss gradient descent and super-critical learning rates as in catapult studies, but focuses on neural quadratic models and their relation to wide neural networks; includes synthetic and CIFAR-2 experiments rather than CIFAR-10/100 classification-error measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning rate changes the dynamics: sub-critical rates give nearly constant kernels and monotonic loss decrease; super-critical rates yield catapult behavior; rates above ηmax diverge. In the multi-example analysis, the eigendirection(s) affected depend on the learning rate interval.
record.problems: The empirical wide-network training-dynamics evidence is presented in figures, without numeric loss values or stated uncertainty in the supplied text. The main theoretical and empirical training results use squared loss and do not measure classification error; some analyses impose unidimensional inputs.
record.rows_left_out: No applicable reported results omitted. Other figures concern test loss/generalization and do not measure the training behavior named by V5.

untested.parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, and model-size, stopping or regularization effects.
Teacher-student spurious local minima and the effect of adding student neurons.
Depth-related training degradation, identity shortcuts, and the stated initialization exceptions.
Comparative effects of activation-matched, Gaussian or orthogonal initialization on training speed and trainable depth.

Long-run loss-Hessian sharpness hovering at the stability threshold and divergence despite an initially sub-threshold rate. The empirical rows primarily track tangent-kernel eigenvalues, rather than directly measuring the full loss Hessian.
Batch normalization versus no normalization and Fixup training speed or stability.

missing.what: A separate divergence result: Theorem 5 proves divergence for the single-example NQM when η≥(4+ϵ)/λ0, with ϵ=Θ(log(m)/√m). It is currently only compressed into R1's baseline.
The post-catapult convergence discussion and zero-loss stable equilibria strengthen the recovery evidence beyond R1's O(1) endpoint.
missing.locator: Section 3.1, discussion after Lemma 2 and Theorem 2

missing.what: Direct experimental verification of NQM loss and eigenvalue dynamics on 128 synthetic examples at width 5,000, distinguishing catapults in one versus two eigendirections.
The corresponding fully connected and convolutional wide-network experiments on 128 SVHN-2 examples are omitted; widths are 2,048 and 1,024 respectively.
Additional NQM experiments report catapults and top-eigenspace loss/kernel dynamics for fully connected and convolutional architectures on CIFAR-2 and SVHN-2.

record.verdict_notes: The record's empirical limits_scope verdict is unwarranted: unavailable numerical plot values do not establish a failure or weakened effect. The text explicitly reports catapults and convergence. These qualitative results support the catapult component of V5 without establishing every component of that version. Tangent-kernel reduction should not be silently equated with a direct full loss-Hessian sharpness measurement.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, random or corrupted labels, model size, and stopping or regularization effects.
Teacher-student two-layer ReLU problems, spurious local minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Depth, plain versus residual networks, and normalization effects on training error.
Comparisons of initialization schemes and their effects on training speed or trainable depth.
The study tests squared-loss catapult dynamics, but does not test sharpness hovering at the stability threshold over longer times or divergence from initial rates below that threshold.
Batch normalization's effect on training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup without normalization.

rows.subject: NQM Eq. (10), approximating a two-layer fully-connected ReLU network
rows.size_stated: width m much larger than input dimension d; d and n treated as small constants
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch gradient descent on squared loss with a super-critical learning rate
rows.baseline: Sub-critical learning rates converge monotonically; η > ηmax diverges
rows.value: Loss increases to order Ω(m(ηλ0−2)^2/log m), then decreases to O(1)
rows.uncertainty: With high probability over random initialization
rows.note: The stated outcome is for a one-example squared-loss NQM, not classification error.
rows.check: Theorem 1 formally requires η in [(2+ϵ)/λ0, (4−ϵ)/λ0], with ϵ=Θ(log(m)/√m), rather than the entire open interval recorded. The subsequent discussion states that training resumes linear convergence after recovery to O(1); Theorem 2 identifies zero-loss stable equilibria. This is a quadratic approximation, not an actual ReLU-network convergence theorem.
